summary: Specifies how to use EdDSA keys and signatures, with Ed25519 and Ed448 curves, in DNSSEC.

plainLanguage.summary: DNS records get a stamp to show they are real. This lets DNS use a modern kind of stamp.

subtitle: How DNSSEC zones can sign their records with the Ed25519 and Ed448 EdDSA algorithms.

tldr.problem: DNSSEC signing was mostly done with RSA, plus GOST and NIST elliptic curves, and had no way to use the EdDSA signature system.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines how Ed25519 and Ed448 public keys go into DNSKEY records and signatures into RRSIG records, and assigns algorithm numbers 15 and 16.
tldr.outcome: DNSSEC signers and validators can use EdDSA. The RFC says Ed25519 is perfectly safe against classical computers, though a large enough quantum computer would break both curves.

today: RFC 8080 is a Proposed Standard, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It defines the DNSSEC algorithms Ed25519 (15) and Ed448 (16) on top of RFC 8032.

sections.title: Adding EdDSA to DNSSEC
sections.content:
DNSSEC uses cryptographic keys and digital signatures to authenticate DNS data. It is broadly defined in RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035. When this RFC was written, RSA was the most popular signature algorithm in use, with GOST (RFC 5933) and NIST elliptic curve cryptography (RFC 6605) also standardized.

RFC 8032 describes the Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA) and recommends two curves, Ed25519 and Ed448. RFC 8080 defines how DNSSEC's DS, DNSKEY and RRSIG records work with EdDSA using either curve.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS already had a few kinds of stamps to prove a record is genuine. This adds a new kind, in two sizes.

sections.title: Public Keys in DNSKEY Records
sections.content:
An Ed25519 public key is a 32-octet value. An Ed448 public key is a 57-octet value. In both cases it is placed in the Public Key field of a DNSKEY record as a simple bit string.

The RFC does not invent a new key format. Key generation is defined in RFC 8032: Section 5.1.5 for Ed25519 and Section 5.2.5 for Ed448.
sections.plainLanguage: The public key is like the pattern of a lock that anyone may look at. It is stored as plain bytes, short for one curve and a bit longer for the other.

sections.title: Signatures in RRSIG Records
sections.content:
An Ed25519 signature is a 64-octet value and an Ed448 signature is a 114-octet value. Each goes into the Signature field of an RRSIG record as a simple bit string.

The signing and verification procedures come straight from RFC 8032: Sections 5.1.6 and 5.1.7 for Ed25519, and Sections 5.2.6 and 5.2.7 for Ed448.
sections.plainLanguage: The signature is the stamp itself, stored as a fixed run of bytes. A bigger stamp means a bigger safety margin.

sections.title: Algorithm Numbers and IANA
sections.content:
The algorithm number is 15 for Ed25519 and 16 for Ed448. The same number is used in DS, DNSKEY and RRSIG records.

The RFC adds both to the IANA registry Domain Name System Security (DNSSEC) Algorithm Numbers. The mnemonics are ED25519 and ED448, and both are marked as usable for zone signing. For transaction security, no determination of standardization has been made.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of stamp gets a number so a record can say which one it uses: 15 for the smaller, 16 for the bigger.

sections.title: Test Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives two sample key sets for each curve. Each shows a private key, a DNSKEY record with flags 257, protocol 3 and the algorithm number, a matching DS record with digest type 2, an MX record and the RRSIG over that MX record, all for example.com. with a TTL of 3600.

Implementers can use them to check that their signing and verification produce matching output.
sections.plainLanguage: The document includes worked answers, like the back of a math book, so builders can check their own results.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 8032 and RFC 7748 are inherited. Ed25519 is intended to operate at around the 128-bit security level and Ed448 at around the 224-bit level. A sufficiently large quantum computer would be able to break both. The RFC calls Ed25519 perfectly safe against reasonable projections of classical computers, and offers Ed448 for applications with relaxed performance requirements that want to hedge against analytical attacks on elliptic curves. It notes these assessments could change if better attacks are found.

A private key used for a DNSSEC zone MUST NOT be used for any other purpose than that zone, otherwise cross-protocol or cross-application attacks are possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Both stamps are very hard to fake today, and the bigger one has extra margin. Never use your zone's secret stamp for anything else.
